title: He will come again (CCC 668–682)
hookLine: Christ reigns now and will come in glory

cards: A group of friends on a hillside outside Jerusalem, heads tipped back, staring at the sky. A cloud has just taken Jesus out of their sight, and they can't stop looking.
Then two men in white are standing beside them, and their question is almost funny.

In the Douay-Rheims: "Ye men of Galilee, why stand you looking up to heaven? This Jesus who is taken up from you into heaven, shall so come, as you have seen him going into heaven." Stop staring, in other words.

teach.b: Day seventy-two stood on that hillside; today, the coming it promises. Parousia is the Church's word, from Greek, for Christ's return in glory at the end of time. But the section opens not with the end but with now.

Christ already reigns, the Catechism says. Since his ascension he is Lord of the world and of history, and his kingdom is already present, in mystery, in the Church, the seed and beginning of that kingdom on earth.
So Catholics live in an in-between: the king already crowned, the kingdom not yet complete. Already, and not yet. And it isn't peaceful.

The kingdom is still under attack by evil, the Catechism says, and the Church will pass through a final trial before the end. Then a line that leaves no room for a calendar: the time of his coming is not known.

teach.h: THE DAY AND THE HOUR: UNKNOWN.
teach.b: Jesus says no one knows the day or the hour, and in Acts he tells the disciples it is not for them to know the times the Father has set.

teach.h: TO JUDGE THE LIVING AND THE DEAD.
teach.b: When he comes, the Creed says, it will be to judge the living and the dead; the Catechism adds that the secrets of hearts will be brought to light. Meanwhile, the Church waits, and the waiting has words.
Near the very end of the Bible, Christ's promise gets an answer, in the Douay-Rheims: "Surely I come quickly: Amen. Come, Lord Jesus."
Catholics hear the same hope at Mass, just after the Our Father, in a prayer that speaks of awaiting the coming of our Savior.

how: Catholics profess at Mass that Christ "will come again in glory to judge the living and the dead," and the season of Advent keeps both his first coming and his return in view.

games.q: you're one of the disciples on the hillside. a cloud has taken Jesus from sight, and two men in white have spoken. what do you do?
o: climb higher for a better look
games.why: Acts says they returned to Jerusalem and gathered to pray. the waiting starts with walking back down.

practice: Look around the day ahead the way a household looks around a room before a guest it loves arrives, not in a panic: a word you'd want to take back, a call you'd want to make, a small mess you'd want set right. Choose just one.
If you pray, say the words near the Bible's end, come, Lord Jesus; if you don't, let the guest be anyone you'd be glad to see walk in.

wordCard.voice: Parousia. Christ's coming in glory at the end of time; he reigns already, and the day is not known. Today's word.

orig.note: the Greek word the Church uses for Christ's return in glory.

carryVoice: Your line: he will come. No date is given, only a hope with words. Until tomorrow.
